Appointed Times
uh-POYNT-ed TYMZ
noun phrase / Hebrew term
Translation of Hebrew mo’adim (singular mo’ed), from the root yā’ad, to appoint or designate by agreement. The term appears first in Genesis 1:14 where God appoints the celestial bodies for “signs and appointed times” — establishing from creation that time itself is divinely ordered, not cyclically indifferent. Leviticus 23:2 applies the term specifically to the sacred calendar of Israel: the mo’adim are the times God appoints for covenant assembly, worship, and commemoration. The English “appointed times” or “feasts of the LORD” preserves the sense of divine initiative: these are not Israel's feasts but the LORD's.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

The appointed times are the sacred seasons that the LORD commanded Israel to observe as covenant assemblies throughout the agricultural and liturgical year — collectively defined in Leviticus 23, Numbers 28–29, and Deuteronomy 16. They include the weekly Sabbath (Lev 23:3), the Passover and Feast of Unleavened Bread (Lev 23:5–8), the Feast of Firstfruits (Lev 23:9–14), the Feast of Weeks / Pentecost (Lev 23:15–22), the Feast of Trumpets / Rosh Hashanah (Lev 23:23–25), the Day of Atonement / Yom Kippur (Lev 23:26–32), and the Feast of Tabernacles / Sukkot (Lev 23:33–43). The LORD identifies them explicitly as “My feasts” (Lev 23:2) — not Israel's religious calendar but the LORD's own appointments within the covenant year. Each feast carries a dual character: it commemorates a historical redemptive event (the Exodus, the wilderness journey, the giving of the law at Sinai) and anticipates a future redemptive fulfillment. This is the typological structure Paul identifies in Colossians 2:17: the feasts are “a shadow of what is to come; but the substance belongs to Christ.” The shadow is real — it was divinely appointed and demanded faithful observance — but the substance that casts the shadow is Christ Himself, whose life, death, resurrection, ascension, and coming return fulfill every feast's anticipatory content. The three pilgrimage feasts (Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles) required every Israelite male to appear before the LORD at the central sanctuary (Deut 16:16) — a tri-annual covenant renewal anchoring the community's common life in the LORD's presence.

Webster 1828 Definition

The appointed times (mo’adim) are the sacred seasons prescribed in Leviticus 23 as the LORD's covenant calendar — seven annual feasts plus the weekly Sabbath — each commemorating past redemptive acts and typologically anticipating their fulfillment in the life and work of Jesus Christ.

APPOINTED TIMES. Hebrew mo’adim (singular mo’ed), from yā’ad, to appoint: the sacred seasons the LORD prescribed for covenant Israel in Leviticus 23 and Numbers 28–29, comprehending the weekly Sabbath and seven annual feast-cycles marking the agricultural and liturgical year.

2. The seven annual mo’adim: (1) Passover / Pesach (Nisan 14); (2) Unleavened Bread / Chag HaMatzot (Nisan 15–21); (3) Firstfruits / Bikkurim (first Sunday after Passover); (4) Weeks / Shavuot / Pentecost (fifty days after Firstfruits); (5) Trumpets / Rosh Hashanah (Tishri 1); (6) Atonement / Yom Kippur (Tishri 10); (7) Tabernacles / Sukkot (Tishri 15–22). Collectively they rehearse the entire arc of redemption in annual cycle.

3. Christological fulfillment (Col 2:17): Passover fulfilled in Christ's crucifixion (1 Cor 5:7); Firstfruits in His resurrection (1 Cor 15:20); Pentecost in the Spirit's outpouring (Acts 2); Atonement in the priestly self-offering (Heb 9:11–12). Trumpets and Tabernacles await final eschatological fulfillment in the second coming and eternal habitation of God with His people.

4. The LORD's ownership: Leviticus 23:2, 4 declares “My feasts” and “feasts of the LORD” — the covenant calendar belongs to God, not to Israel's cultural preference. Observance was obligatory, not optional; non-observance of the Sabbath and pilgrimage feasts carried covenant-curse consequences.

5. New covenant status (Col 2:16–17; Heb 10:1): the substance having come, the shadows are not obligatory on the church. The Council of Jerusalem (Acts 15) and Paul's letters (Gal 4:10; Rom 14:5–6) establish that Gentile believers are not bound to the Mosaic festival calendar, though the typological richness of the feasts remains instructive for understanding the fullness of Christ's redemptive work.

Key Scripture

Lev 23:2 — "Speak to the children of Israel and say to them: The appointed feasts of the LORD which you shall proclaim to be holy convocations, these are My feasts."

Lev 23:4 — "These are the appointed feasts of the LORD, sacred assemblies which you shall proclaim at their appointed times."

Col 2:17 — "things which are a shadow of what is to come; but the substance belongs to Christ."

Zech 14:16 — "And it shall come to pass that everyone who is left of all the nations which came against Jerusalem shall go up from year to year to worship the King, the LORD of hosts, and to keep the Feast of Tabernacles."

Modern Corruption

The appointed times have been corrupted in two directions: by Judaizing movements that impose Mosaic festival observance on the New Testament church as a condition of spiritual maturity, and by Gentile Christianity's wholesale abandonment of the feasts' typological-theological richness, leaving believers without the annual redemptive-historical rehearsal Christ Himself fulfilled at the precise moments each feast anticipated.

expand to see more

Hebrew Roots and Messianic Judaizing movements have reversed the apostolic settlement of Acts 15 and Galatians 4 by requiring Gentile believers to observe the Mosaic calendar as a marker of authentic discipleship and covenant standing. This is precisely the Galatian error Paul calls a return to bondage (Gal 4:9–10). Colossians 2:16 explicitly forbids judging one another over festivals, new moons, or Sabbaths that were shadows; the substance has arrived. The mo’adim were divinely commanded and precious in their appointed season, but their covenant-obligatory force was fulfilled and therefore terminated by the coming of Christ. To reimpose them is not to recover biblical depth but to deny that the substance has come.

The opposite corruption is the evangelical church's poverty-of-ignorance regarding the feasts: treating the Old Testament's liturgical calendar as irrelevant religious history rather than as the typological grammar by which the New Testament's greatest doctrines (incarnation, atonement, resurrection, Pentecost, second coming) are properly understood. A church that has never learned to read Passover is a church that will preach a thinner gospel than Scripture's own. The solution is not to reinstate the feasts as obligatory but to teach their Christological content — to let the shadows teach the shadow's meaning — so that every Good Friday becomes richer because it is understood as Passover fulfilled, and every Pentecost Sunday becomes the outpouring of Shavuot's harvest.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The appointed times root in creation's ordered time (Gen 1:14), in the Exodus commemoration (Passover as the covenant-forming event), in the Sinai legislation (Lev 23; Num 28–29; Deut 16), and in the prophetic eschatological vision of all nations streaming to Jerusalem for the final Feast of Tabernacles (Zech 14:16).

expand to see more

Creation time-order — Gen 1:14: the sun and moon appointed for “signs and appointed times” (mo’adim); the sacred calendar is embedded in the created order of light and time itself, not imposed arbitrarily on history

Exodus Passover — Exod 12: the founding mo’ed from which all others derive; the LORD's deliverance of Israel from Egypt is the paradigm for all subsequent redemptive acts and the primary content of the covenant calendar's memorial structure

Sinai legislation — Lev 23; Num 28–29; Deut 16: the full codification of the seven annual feasts plus the weekly Sabbath as the LORD's comprehensive covenant calendar for Israel in the land

Prophetic eschatology — Zech 14:16–19; Isa 66:23: the feast-structure projected forward into the eschatological age when all nations will worship the King and the entire cosmos will observe the final Sabbath rest

Colossians 2:16–17 and Hebrews 8–10: the New Testament's interpretive key — shadow vs. substance; the feasts were real, divinely appointed, and instructive; their covenant-obligatory force is fulfilled and their typological content is now fully visible in Christ

Usage

"The annual rehearsal of the appointed times gave covenant Israel a structured theological education: each feast cycle re-told the story of redemption, re-enacted the pattern of deliverance, and re-oriented the community toward its future hope. The church that learns to read the mo’adim gains this same structural richness for understanding the full architecture of redemption — creation, fall, exodus, Sinai, atonement, Pentecost, and consummation — rehearsed in annual typological sequence."

"The three pilgrimage feasts (Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles) required every male Israelite to appear before the LORD at the central sanctuary — the covenant community physically gathered at the divine presence. The New Testament fulfills this pattern in the church's weekly gathering before the risen Christ (“where two or three are gathered”, Matt 18:20) and ultimately in the New Jerusalem where the LORD God Almighty is the temple (Rev 21:22)."

"Colossians 2:17 — “the substance belongs to Christ” — is the key that unlocks typological reading of the entire appointed-times calendar. The Christian reads the feasts not as obsolete laws but as revelatory previews: Passover is the cross; Firstfruits is the resurrection; Pentecost is the Spirit's coming; Atonement is the priestly intercession; Tabernacles is the coming eternal dwelling of God with His people. Every feast teaches something about the Christ who came and the Christ who comes."
